The term Hispanic ( ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language)___ : hispano ) refers to people, ___E:cultures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_culture)___ , or countries related to ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain)___ , the ___E:Spanish language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language)___ , or Hispanidad broadly.

In some contexts, ___E:especially within the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans)___ , "Hispanic" is used as an ___E:ethnic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity)___ or ___E:meta-ethnic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-ethnicity)___ term.

The term commonly applies to ___E:Spaniards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards)___ and Spanish-speaking ( ___E:Hispanophone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanophone)___ ) populations and countries in ___E:Hispanic America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_America)___ (the continent) and ___E:Hispanic Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_Africa)___ ( ___E:Equatorial Guinea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_Guinea)___ and the ___E:disputed territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_dispute)___ of ___E:Western Sahara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Sahara)___ ), which were formerly part of the ___E:Spanish Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire)___ due to colonization mainly between the 16th and 20th centuries.

The cultures of Hispanophone countries outside Spain have been influenced as well by the local ___E:pre-Hispanic cultures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era)___ or other foreign influences.

There was also Spanish influence in the former ___E:Spanish East Indies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_East_Indies)___ , including the ___E:Philippines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines)___ , ___E:Marianas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marianas)___ , and other nations.
However, Spanish is not a predominant language in these regions and, as a result, their inhabitants are not usually considered Hispanic.

Hispanic culture is a set of customs, traditions, beliefs, and art forms in music, literature, dress, architecture, cuisine, and other cultural fields that are generally shared by peoples in Hispanic regions, but which can vary considerably from one country or territory to another.
The ___E:Spanish language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language)___ is the main cultural element shared by Hispanic peoples.

The term Hispanic derives from the ___E:Latin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language)___ word Hispanicus , the adjectival derivation of Hispania , which means of the ___E:Iberian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ and possibly ___E:Celtiberian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtiberian_language)___ origin.
In English the word is attested from the 16th century (and in the late 19th century in American English).
The words Spain , Spanish , and Spaniard are of the same etymology as Hispanus , ultimately.
Hispanus was the Latin name given to a person from Hispania during ___E:Roman rule U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire)___ .

The ancient Roman ___E:Hispania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania)___ , which roughly comprised what is currently called the ___E:Iberian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ , included the contemporary states of ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain)___ , ___E:Portugal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal)___ , parts of ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ , ___E:Andorra U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra)___ , and the ___E:British Overseas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Territory)___ of ___E:Gibraltar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar)___ .

In English, the term Hispano-Roman is sometimes used.  The Hispano-Romans were composed of people from many different ___E:Indigenous tribes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Roman_peoples_of_the_Iberian_Peninsula)___ , in addition to colonists from ___E:Italia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Italy)___ .

Some famous Hispani (plural of Hispanus ) and Hispaniensis were the emperors ___E:Trajan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan)___ , ___E:Marcus Aurelius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius)___ , ___E:Hadrian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian)___ , ___E:Theodosius I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I)___ and ___E:Magnus Maximus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Maximus)___ , the poets ___E:Marcus Annaeus Lucanus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Annaeus_Lucanus)___ , ___E:Martial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial)___ and ___E:Prudentius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudentius)___ , the philosophers ___E:Seneca the Elder U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Elder)___ and ___E:Seneca the Younger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger)___ , and the usurper ___E:Maximus of Hispania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximus_of_Hispania)___ .
A number of these men, such as Trajan, Hadrian and others, were in fact descended from Roman colonial families.
Here follows a comparison of several terms related to Hispanic :

Hispania was divided into two provinces: ___E:Hispania Citerior U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Citerior)___ and ___E:Hispania Ulterior U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Ulterior)___ .

In 27 BC, Hispania Ulterior was divided into two new provinces, ___E:Hispania Baetica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Baetica)___ and ___E:Hispania Lusitania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Lusitania)___ , while Hispania Citerior was renamed ___E:Hispania Tarraconensis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Tarraconensis)___ .
This division of Hispania explains the usage of the singular and plural forms (Spain, and The Spains) used to refer to the peninsula and its kingdoms in the Middle Ages.

Before the marriage of Queen ___E:Isabella I of Castile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_I_of_Castile)___ and King ___E:Ferdinand II of Aragon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_II_of_Aragon)___ in 1469, the four Christian kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula—the Kingdom of ___E:Portugal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal)___ , the ___E:Crown of Aragon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon)___ , the ___E:Crown of Castile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile)___ , and the ___E:Kingdom of Navarre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Navarre)___ —were collectively called The Spains.

This revival of the old Roman concept in the ___E:Middle Ages U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages)___ appears to have originated in ___E:Provençal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provence)___ , and was first documented at the end of the 11th century.
In the ___E:Council of Constance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Constance)___ , the four kingdoms shared one vote.
The terms Spain and the Spains were not interchangeable.

Spain was a ___E:geographic territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_region)___ , home to several kingdoms (Christian and Muslim), with separate governments, laws, languages, religions, and customs, and was the historical remnant of the Hispano-Gothic unity.
Spain was not a political entity until much later, and when referring to the Middle Ages, one should not be confounded with the nation-state of today.

The term The Spains referred specifically to a collective of juridico-political units, first the Christian kingdoms, and then the different kingdoms ruled by the same king. Illustrative of this fact is the historical ecclesiastical title of ___E:Primate of the Spains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primacy_of_the_Spains)___ , traditionally claimed by the ___E:Archbishop of Braga U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Braga)___ , a Portuguese prelate.

With the Decretos de Nueva Planta , ___E:Philip V U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Spain)___ started to organize the fusion of his kingdoms that until then were ruled as distinct and independent, but this unification process lacked a formal and juridic proclamation.
Although colloquially and literally the expression "King of Spain" or "King of the Spains" was already widespread,  it did not refer to a unified nation-state.

It was only in ___E:the constitution of 1812 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Constitution_of_1812)___ that was adopted the name Españas (Spains) for the Spanish nation and the use of the title of "king of the Spains".  ___E:The constitution of 1876 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Constitution_of_1978)___ adopts for the first time the name "Spain" for the Spanish nation and from then on the kings would use the title of "king of Spain".

The expansion of the ___E:Spanish Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire)___ between 1492 and 1898 brought thousands of Spanish migrants to the conquered lands, who established settlements, mainly in the Americas, but also in other distant parts of the world (as in the Philippines, the lone Spanish territory in Asia), producing a number of multiracial populations.
Today, the varied populations of these places, including those with Spanish ancestry, are also designated as Hispanic.
The Latin gentile adjectives that belong to Hispania are Hispanus, Hispanicus, and Hispaniensis.
A Hispanus is someone who is a native of Hispania with no foreign parents, while children born in Hispania of Roman parents were Hispanienses .
Hispaniensis means 'connected in some way to Hispania', as in "Exercitus Hispaniensis" ('the Spanish army') or "mercatores Hispanienses" ('Spanish merchants').
Hispanicus implies 'of' or 'belonging to' Hispania or the Hispanus or of their fashion as in "gladius Hispanicus".

The gentile adjectives were not ethnolinguistic but derived primarily on a geographic basis, from the toponym Hispania as the people of Hispania spoke different languages, although Titus Livius ( ___E:Livy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy)___ ) said they could all understand each other, not making clear if they spoke dialects of the same language or were polyglots.

The first recorded use of an ___E:anthroponym U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroponym)___ derived from the toponym Hispania is attested in one of the five fragments, of ___E:Ennius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ennius)___ in 236 BC who wrote "Hispane, non Romane memoretis loqui me" ("Remember that I speak like a Hispanic not a Roman") as having been said by a native of Hispania.

Although sharing the etymology for the word (pt: hispânico , es: hispánico ), the definition for Hispanic is different between Portugal and Spain.

The modern term to identify Portuguese and Spanish territories under a single nomenclature is "Iberian", and the one to refer to cultures derived from both countries in the Americas is "Iberian-American".

These designations can be mutually recognized by people in Portugal and ___E:Brazil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil)___ . "Hispanic" is totally void of any self-identification in Brazil, and quite to the contrary, serves the purpose of marking a clear distinction in relation to neighboring countries' culture.
Brazilians may identify as Latin Americans, but refute being considered Hispanics because their language and culture are neither part of the Hispanic cultural sphere, nor Spanish-speaking world.
In Spanish, the term " hispano ", as in " hispanoamericano ", refers to the people of Spanish origin who live in the Americas and to a relationship to Spain or to the Spanish language.
There are people in Hispanic America that are not of Spanish origin, such as Amerindians- the original people of these areas, as well as Africans and people with origins from other parts of Europe.

Like in Portugal, in the rest of Europe (and wider world) the concept of 'Hispanic' refers to historical ancient Hispania (especially the term Hispano-Roman and Hispania during the Roman Empire) or the Spanish language and cultures shared by all the Spanish-speaking countries.
Both Hispanic and Latino are widely used in American English for Spanish-speaking people and their descendants in the United States.
While Hispanic refers to Spanish speakers overall, Latino refers specifically to people of ___E:Latin American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America)___ descent.
Hispanic can also be used for the people and culture of Spain as well as Latin America.

While originally the term Hispanic referred primarily to the ___E:Hispanos of New Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanos_of_New_Mexico)___ within the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ ,  today, organizations in the country use the term as a broad catchall to refer to persons with a historical and cultural relationship with Spain regardless of race and ethnicity.

The U.S. ___E:Equal Employment Opportunity Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Employment_Opportunity_Commission)___ encourages any individual who believes that he or she is Hispanic to self-identify as Hispanic.

In a recent study, most Spanish speakers of Spanish or Hispanic American descent do not prefer the term Hispanic or Latino when it comes to describing their identity.
Instead, they prefer to be identified by their country of origin.

When asked if they have a preference for either being identified as Hispanic or Latino , the Pew study finds that "half (51%) say they have no preference for either term."  Among those who do express a preference, "'Hispanic' is preferred over 'Latino' by more than a two-to-one margin—33% versus 14%." 21% prefer to be referred to simply as "Americans".
A majority (51%) say they most often identify themselves by their family's country of origin, while 24% say they prefer a pan-ethnic label such as Hispanic or Latino.

Folk and popular dance and music also varies greatly among Hispanics.

For instance, the music from Spain is a lot different from the ___E:Hispanic American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_America)___ , although there is a high grade of exchange between both continents.

On the other side of the ocean, Hispanic America is also home to a wide variety of music, even though Latin music is often erroneously thought of, as a single genre.

Hispanic Caribbean music tends to favor complex polyrhythms of African origin. ___E:Mexican music U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Mexico)___ shows combined influences of mostly European and Native American origin, while traditional Northern Mexican music— ___E:norteño U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norte%C3%B1o_(music))___ and ___E:banda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banda_music)___ — ___E:polka U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polka)___ , has influence from polka music brought by ___E:Central European U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Europe)___ settlers to ___E:Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico)___ which later influenced western music.

The music of Hispanic Americans—such as ___E:tejano music U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tejano_music)___ —has influences in ___E:rock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music)___ , ___E:jazz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz)___ , ___E:R&B U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues)___ , ___E:pop U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_pop)___ , and ___E:country music U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music)___ as well as traditional Mexican music such as ___E:Mariachi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi)___ .

The Spanish and the Portuguese took the ___E:Catholic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church)___ faith to their colonies in the Americas, Africa, and Asia; Catholicism remains the predominant religion amongst most Hispanics.
A small but growing number of Hispanics belong to a ___E:Protestant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism)___ denomination.

Hispanic Christians form the ___E:largest ethno-linguistic group among Christians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_contemporary_ethnic_groups)___ in the world, about 18% of the ___E:world's Christian population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_by_country)___ are Hispanic (around 430 million).
In the United States, some 65% of Hispanics and Latinos report themselves Catholic and 21% Protestant, with 13% having no affiliation.
A minority among the Catholics, about one in five, are ___E:charismatics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charismatic_Christianity)___ .

Among the Protestant, 85% are " ___E:Born-again Christians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_again_(Christianity))___ " and belong to ___E:Evangelical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism)___ or ___E:Pentecostal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostalism)___ churches.
Among the smallest groups, less than 4%, are Jewish.

Among the Spanish-speaking Catholics, most communities celebrate their homeland's ___E:patron saint U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron_saint)___ , dedicating a day for this purpose with festivals and religious services.
Some Spanish-speakers in Latin America syncretize Roman Catholicism and African or Native American rituals and beliefs.

Such is the case of ___E:Santería U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santer%C3%ADa)___ , popular with ___E:Afro-Cubans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cubans)___ , which combines old African beliefs in the form of Roman Catholic saints and rituals.
Other syncretistic beliefs include ___E:Spiritism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kardecist_spiritism)___ and ___E:Curanderismo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curandero)___ .

In Catholic tradition, Our Lady of the Pillar is considered the Patroness of the ___E:Hispanic people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_people)___ and the ___E:Hispanic world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanidad)___ .
While a tiny minority, there are some Muslims in Latin America, in the United States,  and in the Philippines.
Those in the Philippines live predominantly in ___E:Bangsamoro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangsamoro)___ .

There are also Spanish-speaking ___E:Jews U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews)___ , most of whom are the descendants of ___E:Ashkenazi Jews U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jews)___ who migrated from Europe (German Jews, Russian Jews, Polish Jews, etc.) to Hispanic America, particularly ___E:Argentina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina)___ , ___E:Uruguay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay)___ , ___E:Peru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru)___ , and ___E:Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba)___ (Argentina is host to the third-largest Jewish population in the Western Hemisphere, after the United States and Canada)   in the 19th century and following World War II. Many Spanish-speaking Jews also originate from the small communities of reconverted descendants of ___E:anusim U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anusim)___ —those whose Spanish ___E:Sephardi Jewish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardi_Jews)___ ancestors long ago hid their Jewish ancestry and beliefs in fear of persecution by the ___E:Spanish Inquisition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition)___ in the ___E:Iberian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ and Ibero-America.
The Spanish Inquisition led to many forced conversions of Spanish Jews.

Genetic studies on the (male) ___E:Y-chromosome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y_chromosome)___ conducted by the ___E:University of Leeds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leeds)___ in 2008 appear to support the idea that the number of forced conversions have been previously underestimated significantly.
They found that twenty percent of Spanish males have Y-chromosomes associated with Sephardic Jewish ancestry.
This may imply that there were more forced conversions than was previously thought.

There are also thought to be many Catholic-professing descendants of ___E:marranos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrano)___ and Spanish-speaking ___E:crypto-Jews U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypto-Judaism)___ in the ___E:Southwestern United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_United_States)___ and scattered through Hispanic America.

Additionally, there are Sephardic Jews who are descendants of those Jews who fled Spain to Turkey, ___E:Syria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria)___ , and North Africa, some of whom have now migrated to Hispanic America, holding on to some Spanish/Sephardic customs, such as the ___E:Ladino U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaeo-Spanish)___ language, which mixes Spanish, Hebrew, Arabic and others, though written with Hebrew and Latin characters.  ___E:Ladinos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery)___ were also African slaves captive in Spain held prior to the colonial period in the Americas.
